title: LLM Inference Challenges: Understanding vLLM Architecture
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 13)
Understanding vLLM Architecture
In the previous parts, we explored two very important ideas:

Continuous Batching
and
PagedAttention
Continuous batching helped us understand how modern inference systems keep GPUs busy during decode.
PagedAttention helped us understand how KV cache memory can be managed efficiently while requests are constantly entering, growing, and leaving.
At this point, we understand the individual pieces better.
But one question still remains:

How does a real inference engine
combine all of this together?
That leads us to vLLM.
Why talk about vLLM now?
Until now, we have been mostly learning concepts one by one.
We explored:

KV cache
batching
prefill vs decode
continuous batching
PagedAttention
multi-GPU inference
request routing
GPU communication

These are all important. But in real systems, these ideas do not exist separately. They come together inside an inference engine. vLLM is one of the most important open-source examples of this. So this article is not about every detail inside vLLM. Instead, the goal is simpler:
Build a mental model of how vLLM works as a serving engine.
I want to understand where the major pieces fit before jumping into code.
What is vLLM?
At a high level, vLLM is an LLM inference and serving engine.
That means it helps run language models efficiently for real user requests.
A user sends a prompt.

vLLM receives it.
vLLM schedules it.
vLLM runs the model.
vLLM manages KV cache.
vLLM streams tokens back.
So instead of thinking of vLLM as only:
a library to run an LLM
I think it is better to view it as:
a runtime system for serving LLM requests efficiently
That word “runtime” is important. Because vLLM is not just executing one model call. It is continuously managing many requests at the same time.
What problem is vLLM trying to solve?
LLM inference is difficult because requests are dynamic.
One user may send a short prompt.
Another user may send a long prompt.
One request may generate 10 tokens.
Another may generate 1000 tokens.
Some requests finish early.
Some keep running.
Some are waiting.
Some are in prefill.
Some are in decode.
At the same time, the system must manage:

GPU memory
KV cache blocks
batching
scheduling
latency
throughput
token streaming
So vLLM is not only asking:
How do I run the model?
It is also asking:

Which requests should run now?
How much memory do they need?
Can more requests enter?
Which requests have finished?
How do we keep GPUs busy?
How do we avoid wasting KV cache memory?
This is why vLLM architecture matters.
What are the major pieces inside vLLM?
At a high level, we can think of vLLM as having a few major parts:

API Server
Request Queue
Engine Core
Scheduler
KV Cache Manager
Model Executor
GPU Workers
PagedAttention
Output Processor
This may sound like a lot.
But the flow is actually understandable if we follow one request.
What happens when a request arrives?
Suppose a user sends:
"Explain quantum computing in simple terms"
The request first reaches the serving layer. In vLLM, this is usually the API server. The API server is responsible for things like:

receiving the request
parsing the input
tokenizing the prompt
sending work to the engine
streaming generated tokens back
So the API server is the entry point. But the API server itself is not the main brain of inference scheduling. The request must move into the engine. A simple view looks like this:

User
 ↓
API Server
 ↓
Engine Core
 ↓
Scheduler
 ↓
GPU Workers
 ↓
Generated Tokens
What is the engine core?
The engine core is where the main inference loop lives.
This is where vLLM keeps track of active requests, waiting requests, scheduled work, KV cache usage, and model execution.
A useful mental model is:

API Server = receives and returns requests

Engine Core = decides how inference work runs
The engine core is not just passively forwarding requests. It is continuously making scheduling decisions.
It asks:

Which requests are waiting?
Which requests are already running?
Which requests need prefill?
Which requests are decoding?
Which requests finished?
How many tokens can we process now?
Is there enough KV cache memory?
This is where inference starts feeling like a runtime scheduling system.
What does the scheduler do?
The scheduler is one of the most important parts of vLLM. It decides which requests get executed in each step. Earlier, when we discussed continuous batching, we learned that batches are not fixed.

Requests enter.
Requests leave.
The active set keeps changing. The scheduler manages that process. A simple scheduler loop looks like this:

Check waiting requests
Check active requests
Check available KV cache
Choose what runs next
Send work to GPU workers
Receive outputs
Update request states
Repeat
This is why continuous batching belongs naturally inside vLLM.
The scheduler is the component that makes continuous batching practical.
How does this connect to prefill and decode?
Every request usually goes through two broad phases:

Prefill
Decode
During prefill, the prompt is processed. The system creates the initial KV cache for the prompt tokens.
Example:

Prompt tokens:
[T1, T2, T3, T4]

Prefill creates:
KV cache for T1, T2, T3, T4
After prefill, decode begins. During decode, the model generates one token at a time.
Example:

Decode step 1 → generate next token
Decode step 2 → generate next token
Decode step 3 → generate next token
The scheduler must manage both types of work. That is not trivial. Prefill can be large and compute-heavy. Decode is smaller, repeated, and latency-sensitive. So the scheduler must balance:
new requests waiting for first token
with:
active requests waiting for next token
This is where metrics like time to first token and inter-token latency start to make more sense.
Where does KV cache management happen?
Every active request needs KV cache. During prefill, vLLM creates KV cache entries for the prompt. During decode, vLLM appends new KV entries token by token. So memory must be managed continuously.
Example:

Request A enters → allocate KV cache
Request A prefills → store prompt KV
Request A decodes → append new KV
Request A finishes → free KV cache
But vLLM does not want to allocate one huge continuous memory region for every request. That would waste memory. This is where the KV cache manager and PagedAttention become important.
Where does PagedAttention fit?
PagedAttention is the memory idea behind efficient KV cache storage. Instead of storing each request’s KV cache as one large continuous block, the KV cache is divided into smaller blocks.
A request sees a logical sequence:

Token 1
Token 2
Token 3
Token 4
But physically, its KV cache blocks may live in different places in GPU memory.
Example:

Logical KV blocks:
[A0][A1][A2]

Physical memory:
[A1][B0][free][A0][C0][A2]

The system keeps track of where the blocks are. So the request can still use its KV cache correctly, even if the physical memory is not continuous. This is the bridge between Part 12 and vLLM architecture.
PagedAttention is not floating separately.
It supports the scheduler by making KV cache allocation more flexible.
Why does the scheduler need the KV cache manager?
The scheduler cannot simply admit every request. Before adding more work, it must know whether there is enough KV cache space.
For example:

Waiting requests:
E, F, G

Active requests:
A, B, C, D

Free KV blocks:
limited
The scheduler must ask:

Can E fit?
Can F fit?
Should G wait?
Do active requests need more blocks?
Did any request finish and free blocks?
So scheduling and memory management are tightly connected. This is a key idea.
In LLM inference, scheduling is not only about compute. It is also about memory.
What are GPU workers?
Eventually, the work must run on GPUs. That is where GPU workers come in.
A simple mental model is:

Engine Core
 ↓
GPU Workers
 ↓
Model Execution

The engine core decides what should run. The GPU workers execute model computation. They load model weights, run forward passes, and manage GPU-side execution. If there are multiple GPUs, vLLM may use distributed execution strategies such as tensor parallelism.
But for this article, the important idea is simple:

Scheduler decides the work.
GPU workers execute the work.
What happens during one inference step?
Let us simplify one engine step. Suppose the system currently has active requests:
A, B, C
And waiting requests:
D, E
The scheduler checks:

A needs next decode token
B needs next decode token
C needs next decode token
D needs prefill
E is waiting
It also checks memory:

Are KV cache blocks available?
Can D be admitted?
Can active requests continue?
Then it creates a plan for the next step.
Example:

Run decode for A, B, C
Run prefill chunk for D
Keep E waiting
Then the work is sent to GPU workers.

The model runs.
Outputs come back.
The scheduler updates states.
Example:

A generated one token
B generated one token
C finished
D completed part of prefill
C's KV blocks can be freed
E may enter next step
Then the loop continues. This is the heart of an inference engine.
How does continuous batching appear inside this loop?
Continuous batching means the active batch can change between generation steps.
In vLLM, this is naturally handled by the scheduler.
Example:

Step 1:
Active = [A, B, C, D]

Step 2:
C finishes
E enters

Active = [A, B, D, E]

Step 3:
A finishes
F enters

Active = [F, B, D, E]
The key idea is:

The batch is not frozen.
The scheduler keeps updating it.
This is why vLLM can keep GPUs more fully utilized.
It does not wait for an entire static batch to finish before admitting new work.
How does PagedAttention support this loop?
Continuous batching makes memory dynamic. PagedAttention makes dynamic memory easier to manage. Without PagedAttention, the system may struggle with:

fragmentation
over-allocation
wasted KV cache memory
limited active batch size
With PagedAttention, vLLM can allocate KV cache in smaller blocks. When a request grows, it gets more blocks. When a request finishes, its blocks return to the free pool. Example:

A finishes → free A's blocks
E enters → allocate blocks to E
B grows → allocate one more block to B
So the scheduler and memory manager work together. Continuous batching asks:
Can we add more useful work?
PagedAttention helps answer:
Do we have memory blocks available for that work?
What is the model executor?
The model executor is the part responsible for actually running the model computation.
The scheduler does not itself multiply matrices.
The KV cache manager does not itself generate tokens.
Those components decide what should happen and how memory should be organized.
The model executor runs the forward pass.
A simplified view:

Scheduler
 ↓
Model Executor
 ↓
GPU Workers
 ↓
Forward Pass
 ↓
Logits
 ↓
Sampling
 ↓
Next Token
After the model produces logits, vLLM still needs to choose the next token.
That may involve sampling settings like:

temperature
top-p
top-k
max tokens
stop conditions
Then the generated token is returned to the request state. If streaming is enabled, it can be sent back to the user.
What does the full request lifecycle look like?
Now we can connect the full flow.

User sends prompt
 ↓
API Server receives request
 ↓
Prompt is tokenized
 ↓
Request enters engine
 ↓
Scheduler decides when it runs
 ↓
KV cache blocks are allocated
 ↓
Prefill processes prompt
 ↓
Initial KV cache is created
 ↓
Request enters decode loop
 ↓
Continuous batching keeps active set full
 ↓
PagedAttention manages KV cache blocks
 ↓
GPU workers execute model forward passes
 ↓
Sampler selects next tokens
 ↓
Tokens stream back to user
 ↓
Request finishes
 ↓
KV cache blocks are freed
This is the mental model I wanted. vLLM is not one single trick. It is a system where many pieces work together.
Why is this architecture powerful?
The power comes from combining multiple optimizations into one runtime.

Continuous batching improves GPU utilization.
PagedAttention improves KV cache memory efficiency.
The scheduler coordinates active and waiting requests.
The KV cache manager tracks memory availability.
GPU workers execute the model efficiently.
The API server handles client-facing request and response flow.
Together, these pieces turn LLM inference into a managed runtime system.
That is very different from simply calling:
model.generate()
Why is this different from a simple inference script?
In a simple script, we may do:

load model
send prompt
generate output
return response
That is fine for learning. But production serving is different. A real serving system may have:

many users
many active requests
different prompt lengths
different output lengths
streaming responses
GPU memory limits
parallel GPUs
latency targets
throughput targets
So the problem becomes much larger than running one forward pass. The system must operate continuously. This is why vLLM feels more like an operating system for inference workloads.
It manages compute, memory, scheduling, and execution.
What should we not overcomplicate yet?
At this point, I do not want to dive too deeply into every internal class or source file. That will come later.
For now, the important mental model is:

API Server receives requests.
Engine Core manages inference.
Scheduler decides what runs.
KV Cache Manager manages memory.
PagedAttention stores KV cache efficiently.
GPU Workers execute model computation.
Tokens are streamed back.
This is enough to start reading the vLLM codebase more comfortably later. Without this map, the source code can feel overwhelming. With this map, each component has a place.
How do the previous articles connect now?
Part 10 explained:
Prefill vs Decode
Part 11 explained:
Continuous Batching
Part 12 explained:
PagedAttention
Now Part 13 connects them:

vLLM uses these ideas together
inside a real inference engine.
The picture becomes:

Prefill creates KV cache.
Decode generates one token at a time.
Continuous batching keeps decode efficient.
PagedAttention keeps KV cache memory efficient.
The scheduler coordinates everything.
GPU workers execute the model.
This is the architecture-level understanding.
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize vLLM like this:

vLLM is a scheduling + memory management + model execution system
for high-throughput LLM serving.
Or even simpler:

vLLM keeps GPUs busy
and keeps KV cache memory efficient
while serving many dynamic requests.
That is the core idea.
Why does this article matter?

This article feels like a transition point. Before this, I was mostly learning separate concepts. Now those concepts are starting to form a system. vLLM gives us a concrete place to connect them. It shows why inference is not only about model architecture. It is also about runtime architecture. The model is important. But the serving engine decides how efficiently that model can serve real users.
What comes next?
Now that the high-level vLLM architecture is clearer, the next step is to go one level deeper.
The most natural next topic is:
Inside the vLLM Scheduler
Because the scheduler is where many important decisions happen:

Which requests enter?
Which requests wait?
How are prefill and decode balanced?
How is the token budget used?
How does the system protect latency?
How does it keep throughput high?
How does it work with KV cache limits?
After that, we can go deeper into:

KV cache block manager
request lifecycle
chunked prefill
prefix caching
running vLLM locally
reading vLLM source code
And this is also where I think the series can start becoming more hands-on.
The conceptual foundation is finally strong enough.
Now the next step is to connect this mental model with actual implementation, experiments, and code.
